newsitem.title: GERMANY: Socialists, German unions call for Euro jobs pact.
newsitem.headline: Socialists, German unions call for Euro jobs pact.

text.p: French and German socialist leaders urged on Wednesday the creation of a European "employment pact" as workers across Germany held rallies against unemployment and called on European governments to end cost-cutting measures.

French Socialist leader Lionel Jospin and his German counterpart, Social Democrat (SPD) chief Oskar Lafontaine, said in a joint statement that Europe's monetary union could only benefit its citizens if accompanied by concrete measures to reduce the current 18 million unemployed across the continent.

They called on the European Council of Ministers to include employment targets in "the front line of its decision-making" and for a specific chapter on jobs policy to be included in the Maastricht Treaty, the guidebook for European monetary union.

German union leaders at a Frankfurt news conference to mark a day of rallies throughout Europe called "Europe needs work" reaffirmed the goals of Jospin and Lafontaine in calling for increased government spending to create new jobs.

"I leave open if the view has finally taken hold that unemployment has become the central threat to our European society or if the fact has sunken in that many European people are sending away conservative governments," Dieter Schulte, president of the DGB German union told a news conference.

Schulte, along with DAG union chief Roland Issen, called on Bonn to increase spending to fuel Germany's economic recovery despite Bonn's goals of reaching deficit level criteria in the Maastricht Treaty for entry into currency union.

DGB officials said rallies were held on Wednesday in 23 European countries, including one in Frankfurt by about 40 people in front of the Frankfurt headquarters of the European Monetary Institute, forerunner to the European Central Bank.

Lafontaine and Jospin called for increased training opportunities and a requirement on trade unions and employers that wage and employment policies be focussed on ways to create more jobs through the use of productivity gains.
They also said corporate taxes should also be harmonised across the continent to prevent so-called "tax-dumping" where employers flock to areas with the most favourable tax rates.

"Monetary union is no end in itself. The euro will only meet with the approval of Europe's citizens if currency union promotes growth, employment and stability in all member states," the two opposition leaders said.
